hub.description: Decks and fences in Columbia, TN, from older homes near the square to new yards on the edge of town, with notes on rock, river lots, and HOAs.
hub.intro: Columbia backyards tend to fall into two groups. Near the square and along older streets like West Seventh, many houses have stood for decades, and the deck out back may have been patched more than once. Out toward the edges of town, many newer subdivisions start with a bare clay yard and a set of HOA rules. We build decks and fences for homeowners in both situations. This page covers what usually matters in Columbia before you ask anyone for a price.

sections.heading: Older Columbia houses and the decks behind them
paragraphs: Many older Columbia houses were built before backyard decks were common, so the deck out back was added later. The weak spot is usually where the deck meets the wall. If the board fastened to the house was never flashed, water has been getting behind it for years, and rot can start there well before it shows on top. Once the framing is soft, new boards only hide the problem. At that point, replacing the deck from the footings up is usually the safer choice. Our page on [deck building in Columbia](/deck-builder-columbia-tn/) goes into what that involves.

sections.heading: Newer yards on the edges of town
paragraphs: Columbia keeps growing outward, and a lot of the newer neighborhoods sit on land that was farmed or pastured not long ago. Those yards usually begin as graded clay with sod rolled over it. Soil pushed up against a new foundation can keep settling for a while, so deck footings need to go past it into firm ground. Look at the back and side lot lines too. Some lots have a shallow swale there to carry storm water, and a fence built tight across it can hold water back.

Many of these Columbia subdivisions have an HOA, and those HOAs usually want to approve a fence or deck before work starts. Expect questions about style and color, plus how far forward along the side of the house the fence can run. Get that approval in writing first. Our guide to [getting HOA approval for a fence or deck](/guides/hoa-approval-deck-fence/) shows what a clean submission looks like, and our page on [fence installation in Columbia](/fence-company-columbia-tn/) covers the rest.

sections.heading: Clay and limestone under Maury County yards
paragraphs: Dig a post hole in many Columbia yards and you hit sticky clay first. In many spots there is limestone not far below it. One hole can go down clean while the next stops on rock that has to be drilled or broken out. Clay also holds water after a rain, which is hard on wood set in the ground. Posts last longer when the bottom of the hole drains and the top sheds water away. Gate posts show the problem first. When a gate starts dragging or will not latch, the post holding it may have shifted in the clay. Ask any builder how they plan to handle rock before the job starts, not after the first hole.

sections.heading: Lots along the Duck River
paragraphs: The Duck River runs along the north edge of downtown Columbia, and homes near it bring their own questions. Some of those lots fall inside mapped flood areas, where a deck or fence may need extra review before it can be built. Ground near the water tends to stay soft longer after heavy rain, which matters for footings and gate posts alike. Many of these lots slope toward the river, so a deck can end up well off the ground on the low side. If your lot backs up to the water or a low spot that floods, mention it when you ask for an estimate.

sections.heading: Permits and historic review in Columbia
paragraphs: Rules for decks and fences are not the same everywhere, and in Columbia they depend on where your lot sits. Inside the city limits, you will be dealing with the City of Columbia. Outside them, it is usually Maury County. Parts of downtown Columbia and some older streets nearby fall under historic review, and changes that show from the street may need design approval before work begins. A new front yard fence is a common example. Call the codes office before you settle on a plan, and read your HOA covenants if you have them. Rules change from time to time, so a quick call is worth it even if a neighbor built the same thing a while back.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a deck or fence in Columbia?
faqs.a: It depends on the project and where you live. Most raised or attached decks need a permit and inspections. Fences are often simpler, though a historic district or an HOA can add a step. Start with the City of Columbia codes office if you are inside the city limits, or with Maury County if you are not. Our guide to [deck permits in Tennessee](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) explains the general process.

faqs.q: Is the old deck on my older Columbia house worth saving?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If the framing and the connection to the house are solid, new boards and railings can buy it more years. On a lot of older houses in Columbia, though, the trouble is underneath, and the deck may not be fastened to the house the way decks are built now. When the structure itself is worn out, repairs tend to keep coming, and replacing it is often the better long term choice. Have someone look under it before you decide.

faqs.q: We just moved into a new build in Columbia. Should the fence or the deck come first?
faqs.a: If you have a dog and a bare yard, the fence usually comes first. It still helps to plan both at the same time. Decide where the deck stairs will land and where a gate makes sense, so the fence does not box in the deck later. If your neighborhood has an HOA, try to submit both projects together. That way the committee sees the whole plan at once, not two pieces months apart.

deck.description: Deck builder in Columbia, TN. What to know about replacing old decks on older homes, footings in Maury County rock, and building on newer lots.
deck.intro: If you are looking for a deck builder in Columbia, start with the house you have. Behind an older house, the deck may have gone soft underfoot and started to pull away from the wall. Behind a newer one, the back door may step straight down onto bare grass. Both are common around town. The work is different for each, and so are the questions worth asking before anyone starts digging.

sections.heading: Replacing an old deck in Columbia
paragraphs: On older houses in and around downtown Columbia, the deck has often aged worse than the house itself. Many were built before today's rules for how a deck attaches to a house, and that connection is where they tend to fail. Look for dark, soft wood along the house side and posts sitting right in the dirt. Nails where you would expect bolts are another bad sign. When more than one of these shows up, you are usually looking at a replacement, not a repair.

Tearing out the old deck also gives you a clean start. Many older decks were sized around a small back door and a grill, and people want more room now. You can move the stairs to a better spot or add a lower level that steps down toward the yard. Hauling off the old lumber is part of the job, so ask any deck builder you talk to whether removal is in their price. Our guide on [signs your deck is done](/guides/signs-you-need-a-new-deck/) covers the warning signs in more detail.

sections.heading: How a new deck meets an older house
paragraphs: Older Columbia homes come with details that shape the plan. Many older houses around town have brick veneer, and a deck ledger should not be fastened to it, so those decks usually get their own beam and posts along the house side instead. On houses with wood or fiber cement siding, the siding comes off where the ledger goes so it can be bolted to the framing and flashed properly. Many older houses sit over a crawlspace, so the back door can be well above the yard. That means more steps and a railing, and it is worth thinking early about where those stairs land.

sections.heading: Footings in Columbia clay and rock
paragraphs: In Columbia, footings are often the slowest part of a deck job. The clay here is dense and holds water. Below it, limestone can show up at uneven depths, sometimes near the surface in one hole and nowhere in the next. A footing has to reach the depth your codes office requires, and it has to bear on solid ground. When a hole stops on rock, how that is handled is up to the inspector, so it pays to plan for it before digging starts.

Many builders now stand posts on top of the footings instead of burying them in the clay. Wood left in wet soil rots faster, even lumber rated for ground contact. A metal post base holds the wood up off the concrete so it can dry between rains. It is a small detail that helps posts last longer in this ground.

sections.heading: Decks for newer homes around Columbia
paragraphs: New houses on the edges of Columbia often come with a small concrete patio or just a door and a few steps. Many of those yards get full sun, since trees were often cleared when the lots were graded. That affects your choice of boards. Darker composite gets hot on a summer afternoon, and pressure treated pine left unstained dries out and cracks faster with no shade. Our comparison of [wood vs composite decking](/guides/wood-vs-composite-decking/) lays out the tradeoffs. Think about where the shade will fall at the hour you plan to sit outside.

If you have an HOA, the deck will likely need approval before work starts. Committees in newer neighborhoods tend to ask about railing and stain colors and whether the deck can be seen from the street. Fill soil near the foundation of a new house can settle for a while after construction, so footings close to the house need to reach undisturbed ground. A careful deck builder keeps digging until the hole reaches firm, undisturbed soil.

sections.heading: Decks on river lots and sloped yards
paragraphs: Homes near the Duck River and on the hillier parts of Columbia often have a yard that falls away from the house. That can mean a deck well off the ground on the back side, with tall posts and cross bracing, plus stairs that may need a landing partway down. Plan the stairs early on these lots, because a long run of steps takes up a lot of yard. Lots in mapped flood areas can face added review, and soft ground near the water calls for footings that reach firmer soil. Check with the city, or Maury County outside the limits, before you settle on a size.

sections.heading: Permits, historic review, and getting a price
paragraphs: Most decks that attach to the house or stand well off the ground need a permit. In Columbia, the city handles that inside the limits, and Maury County usually covers homes outside them. If your house sits in one of the local historic districts, a rear deck may draw less review than a change to the front of the house, but do not assume. Call first. Our guide to [deck permits in Tennessee](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) explains how the process usually works.

When you ask for an estimate, a few details help. Tell us whether an old deck has to come off first and how high the door sits above the yard. Mention it if you already know about rock or soft ground. Side yards on older lots can be narrow, so let us know if a fence or a detached garage limits access to the back. You can [request a deck estimate](#estimate) right on this page.

faqs.q: Can the footings from my old deck be reused?
faqs.a: Usually not. Footings under older decks around Columbia were often small and shallow, and some posts were simply set in the ground. They may not meet what the inspector expects today, and they rarely line up with a new layout anyway. New footings are a small part of the job and the hardest part to fix later. If the old ones happen to be sound and in the right place, that is a bonus, but plan on new ones.

faqs.q: Does a deck behind a house in a Columbia historic district need approval?
faqs.a: It might. Historic review usually focuses on what people can see from the street, so a deck tucked behind the house often gets less attention than a change to the front of the house. Corner lots and wide side yards change that, because the deck may be visible. The city can tell you whether your project needs design review. Ask before you settle on materials or a railing style, since those are the details a review is likely to look at.

faqs.q: What decking holds up best in a Columbia summer?
faqs.a: Pressure treated pine is the most common choice and costs the least up front, but it needs cleaning and a fresh coat of stain every few years. Cedar looks warmer and weighs less, with similar upkeep. Composite boards resist rot and skip the staining, though darker colors get hot in full sun. On a new lot with no shade yet, that heat matters more than most people expect.

faqs.q: My Columbia yard drops off toward the river. Can it still have a deck?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. A sloped yard means taller posts and more bracing, with footings set down into firm soil below the soft layer near the surface. If the lot is near the Duck River, find out whether it sits in a mapped flood area, because that can add a review step. The upside is that a raised deck on a slope often gets the best view on the property.

faqs.q: How much does a new deck cost in Columbia?
faqs.a: It depends mostly on the deck you want and the yard it goes in. Size and height move the price most. The board material and railing style come next. Tearing out an old deck adds cost, and so does rock in the footing holes, which turns up often around Columbia. When you compare bids, check that each one includes removal and the same stairs and railing, so you are comparing the same deck.

fence.description: Fence installation in Columbia, TN, for new subdivisions with HOA rules, older lots near downtown, and yards dug into Maury County clay and rock.
fence.intro: Plenty of people calling a fence company in Columbia want a safe place to let the dog out, some privacy from the house next door, or both. Where your house sits in town changes how the fence gets built. An older lot near downtown may have big tree roots and corner pins nobody has seen in years. A newer yard on the edge of town often comes with HOA rules and clay that turns slick after a storm. Here is what matters for fence installation in each case.

sections.heading: Privacy fences in newer Columbia subdivisions
paragraphs: In the newer neighborhoods around Columbia, a privacy fence is often the first project after closing. Before anything else, read your HOA covenants. Many spell out the allowed styles and stain colors and how far toward the street a fence can come. Some want the finished side facing out. Send the request with a simple drawing of the fence line and a photo of the style, and wait for written approval before any posts go in.

New lots in Columbia bring a couple of site issues. Many have a utility easement along the back line, and what you can build inside it is often limited. If a neighbor already has a fence on the shared line, you may be able to tie into it with their permission, or run your own line just inside yours. Bare clay yards also settle, so posts set soon after grading need to reach past the loose fill. Our guide to [privacy fence options](/guides/privacy-fence-options/) compares the common styles.

sections.heading: Fencing older lots near downtown Columbia
paragraphs: On established lots near downtown and along West Seventh, the property line is not always where the old fence says it is. Corner pins get buried or pulled over the decades. Before new fence installation on an older Columbia lot, find the pins or get a survey. A survey usually costs less than moving a fence later. Our guide to [fences and property lines in Tennessee](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) walks through how to handle it, including talking with the neighbor before work starts.

Big trees are the other issue on older lots. Mature trees near the line can have roots that fill the post holes, and cutting a large root can hurt the tree. It is usually better to shift a post or change the spacing than to cut through a big root. If your house is in a historic district, a fence in the front or side yard may need design review before it goes up. The city can tell you whether your lot falls inside one.

sections.heading: Setting posts in Maury County clay and rock
paragraphs: A fence is only as straight as its posts, and the ground in Columbia makes posts the hardest part of the job. Clay swells when it is wet and shrinks when it dries, and over time that movement can push a shallow post out of line. Limestone is the other surprise. An auger can run clean for a few holes and then stop cold on rock, and that hole has to be drilled out or shifted a little. Before any of it, call Tennessee 811 so buried lines get marked.

A few habits help posts last in this ground. The hole goes deep enough for the fence height and the wind it will catch. Gravel at the bottom lets water drain instead of sitting against the wood. Concrete, if used, is shaped so water runs away from the post at the top. Gate posts carry the most strain, so they usually get deeper, wider holes. Ask any fence company how they set posts in clay before you hire them.

sections.heading: Fences near the Duck River and low ground
paragraphs: If your Columbia yard is near the Duck River or backs up to a creek that rises, a solid privacy fence can act like a wall when water moves through. It catches debris, and the moving water pushes against it. Some owners in these spots choose a style with open spacing low down, or they leave the flood path open and fence around it. Lots in mapped flood areas may need extra review before building anything, so ask the city first. Soft ground near water also calls for deeper posts at gates and corners.

sections.heading: Larger lots outside the Columbia city limits
paragraphs: Plenty of homes around Columbia sit on larger lots out in the county. On land like that, many people do not fence the whole property. Instead they fence a yard around the house for the dogs and the kids, with a gate wide enough for a mower. Long open runs catch more wind, which is one more reason to set posts well. Outside the city limits, Maury County rules usually apply instead of the city's, and deed restrictions can matter too.

sections.heading: What goes into a fence price
paragraphs: Length drives most of the cost, and height and style come next. Gates add more than people expect, because each one needs heavy posts and hardware. Tearing out an old fence adds time, and so does hitting rock in the post holes, which is common around Columbia. When you ask for an estimate, tell us roughly how much yard you want enclosed and how many gates you need. Mention any HOA rules you already know about. You can [start a fence estimate](#estimate) on this page.

faqs.q: Do I need a survey before fence installation in Columbia?
faqs.a: Not always, but it is the safest start on an older lot. If you can find the metal pins at each corner and they match your plat, that may be enough. When the pins are missing or the old fence wanders, a survey settles it. Most owners keep the fence just inside their own line, and fixing a mistake later means pulling posts. Your HOA may also ask for a plot plan showing the fence line.

faqs.q: How tall can a privacy fence be in Columbia?
faqs.a: That depends on where the fence goes and who sets the rules. City zoning usually limits fence height, with lower limits in front yards than in back. Many HOAs are stricter than the city and spell out a height in their covenants. Historic districts can add their own design rules on top. Check with the City of Columbia codes office, or Maury County if you live outside the city, before you order materials.

faqs.q: Does a fence near downtown Columbia need historic approval?
faqs.a: It can. If your house is inside one of the local historic districts, a new fence that shows from the street may need design review before it goes up. Style and material both tend to matter. A fence hidden in the backyard is less likely to draw review, but corner lots are harder to hide. The city can tell you whether your address falls in a district and what the review involves.

faqs.q: Can a fence cross the drainage swale behind my Columbia house?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but it should not block the water. Swales in newer subdivisions often carry storm runoff from several yards, and a solid fence across one can back water up into your yard or your neighbor's. The usual answer is a gap at the bottom where the swale runs, or a short open section there. Some HOAs and easements limit what can be built in the swale at all, so check your plat and covenants first.

faqs.q: We just built in Columbia and are putting in a new yard. Should the fence go in first?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Fence posts and panels take room to install, and a crew working along the line can crush new beds and shrubs. Setting the fence first also shows you where the beds should go. The exception is regrading. If the yard still needs dirt work or a drainage fix, get that done before the posts go in, because moving the ground later can leave posts too shallow or gaps under the boards.
